title: Tuning Quantum MPS
authors: Anna Leonteva, Maxime Outteryck, Guido Masella
abstract: Matrix Product State (MPS) methods are among the most effective approaches for the classical simulation of quantum circuits, but their practical performance depends strongly on simulator hyperparameters, and default settings are often suboptimal. In this work, we propose a two-stage framework for automatic hyperparameter selection for quantum MPS simulation. In the first stage, we perform offline single-objective CMA-ES optimization under a fidelity constraint and construct a database of circuit--configuration--performance evaluations. In the second stage, we define a set of static circuit features designed to capture MPS-relevant structural properties and train a circuit-aware hybrid ranking model to recommend configurations for different quantum circuits. We evaluate the approach on multiple scalable circuit families using leave-one-family-out and size-based validation. The results show that offline optimization often improves over default settings, although the magnitude of the gain depends strongly on the backend, circuit family, and circuit scale. The learned predictor recovers a meaningful fraction of this gain, with better performance under size-based validation than under family-based transfer, but generally remains below the offline optimum.
summary: The paper introduces a novel two-stage framework to automate hyperparameter tuning for MPS simulations of quantum circuits. It first optimizes settings offline using CMA-ES and then trains a hybrid ranking model on circuit features to predict optimal configurations for new circuits. This allows researchers to efficiently manage the complex, high-dimensional search space inherent in state-of-the-art quantum simulation techniques.
main_problem: The core problem is developing an automated, data-driven method to select optimal hyperparameters for Matrix Product State (MPS) simulation of quantum circuits.
main_result: A two-stage framework combining offline CMA-ES optimization with a circuit-aware hybrid ranking model can predict good configurations, recovering a meaningful fraction of the performance gain over default settings.
method: The approach uses an initial offline optimization phase to build a database, followed by training a complex ensemble ranking model on static circuit features to predict optimal parameters for unseen circuits.
model_or_system: The system under study is the simulation of quantum circuits using the Matrix Product State (MPS) method across various quantum backends (Qiskit and MIMIQ).
key_observables: Run time ($T$), Fidelity ($F$), run time ratio ($r$), and fidelity gap ($\Delta F$).

main_assumptions: The prediction model's performance is compared against an ideal offline optimum, and size-based validation was found to be more reliable than family-based transfer.
figures_summary: Figures compare speedup distributions from offline optimization across circuit families for Qiskit and MIMIQ, and show the predictive model's speedup under one-family-out vs. size-based validation.
paper_structure: The paper details a two-stage process: first, building an optimization database via CMA-ES; second, training a hybrid ranking model using circuit features to predict optimal configurations for generalization.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of simulating complex quantum dynamics by providing a machine learning tool to optimize simulation parameters, which is crucial for scaling tensor network methods.

Figure 1 compares the distribution of offline optimization speedup across circuit families for Qiskit and MIMIQ. Speedup is defined as the ratio of default to optimized run time, so values above one indicate improvement. For each circuit family, the box plot aggregates the speedup values obtained for the available circuit instances at different qubit counts. The central line indicates the median, the box spans the interquartile range, and the whiskers show the spread of the observed values. Compact distributions indicate more consistent gains across instances, whereas wider ones indicate larger variability with circuit size. The two backends exhibit clearly different behavior.
